newsitem.title: CANADA: Stars obey Toronto smoking ban, natives howl.
newsitem.headline: Stars obey Toronto smoking ban, natives howl.

text.p: Canada's largest city has enacted one of North America's toughest anti-smoking laws, barring even movie star and cigar aficionado Demi Moore from lighting up at her trendy new Toronto restaurant.
At a party on Monday night to open Toronto's Planet Hollywood, a restaurant chain in which she is part owner along with fellow cigar buff Arnold Schwarzenegger, Moore accepted the ban with a shrug.
"I guess I'm not going to smoke because I wouldn't want to break the law," Moore, the star of "Striptease" and "Ghost", told reporters at the party.
But other smokers are not as placid about the controversial law banning smoking in all Toronto bars and restaurants, surpassing similar measures in U.S. cities such as Los Angeles and New York.
Rosie Dimanno, a columnist at Canada's biggest newspaper, The Toronto Star, took aim at what she called an "ill-advised, sanctimonious, and thuggish bylaw."
"And the smoke police can kiss my butt," she wrote.
The measure, which its framers said was designed to protect people from the effects of second-hand smoke, was passed last October and took effect on Monday.

Owners and managers of Toronto's $735 million restaurant industry complain that the law goes too far in ordering bars and restaurants either to ban smoking or build separate ventilated rooms for smokers not exceeding 25 percent of the total seating space.
Toronto restaurant owners predict a 20 to 30 percent drop in business as patrons seek out bars in the suburbs, which are not covered by the ban.
North York, a suburban city north of Toronto, repealed a similar ban a few years ago after its restaurants experienced heavy losses.
"People that were implementing the ban to 100 percent were experiencing a 20 to 30 percent reduction of business," said Ken Baxter, chairman of the Ontario Restaurant Association.

Mike O'Connor, manager of Joe Badali's restaurant in downtown Toronto, said his business had fallen by more than 20 percent since the ban was imposed on Monday despite the restaurant's having a legal smoking room.

"Once a smoker gets it into his mind that he can't smoke in the city of Toronto, it's going to be hard to get him to come back," O'Connor said. "We're going to lose business because city councillors made it their mission to try and get people to quit smoking."

Breaking the law has become an instant sport in local bars, with many smokers flaunting their habit and risking fines of up to $2,700 from 25 municipal health officers policing Toronto's 4,500 restaurants and bars.
Unless the city council relents, Torontonians may seek to emulate actor Tom Arnold, who stood outside the Planet Hollywood party fighting the wind to light his cigar.
